text: A longer duration of immediate mother-newborn skin-to-skin contact was associated with higher odds of breastfeeding initiation among neonates delivered vaginally. Immediate mother-newborn skin-to-skin contact (SSC) supports neonatal adaptation and breastfeeding, but the association between SSC duration and breastfeeding outcomes remains unclear.

Cracking the fertility code: a comprehensive review of biomarkers and functional measures. Human fertility is regulated by a complex, integrated network of biological systems that collectively determine reproductive competence in males and females. Conventional fertility assessment relies on established clinical biomarkers, including reproductive hormone profiles, gamete-based functional assessments and imaging indicators of gonadal structure and function. While clinically informative, these measures capture only partial views of molecular and cellular processes underlying gametogenesis and reproductive capacity. Recent advances in reproductive medicine have expanded the biomarker landscape through genetic and epigenetic profiling, enabling identification of pathogenic variants, chromosomal abnormalities and regulatory modifications associated with infertility syndromes. In parallel, multi-omics approaches are increasingly being used to characterize molecular networks governing gamete development, meiotic integrity, DNA repair and cellular differentiation. This review presents a comprehensive synthesis of fertility biomarkers, spanning endocrine, genetic, epigenetic, structural, metabolic and inflammatory systems. Current evidence is examined on endocrine and reproductive hormone biomarkers, followed by an investigation of genetic and epigenetic markers of reproductive dysfunction, as well as structural and imaging-based biomarkers and inflammatory and metabolic indicators. Finally, emerging biomarker platforms are highlighted as key advances towards precision reproductive medicine. Collectively, these developments support a shift towards a more comprehensive, biomarker-driven framework for the evaluation and management of infertility.

Transcriptional activation of the CXCL gene family locus in mature human sperm in the presence of female-derived reproductive fluid. Mature sperm are widely considered as transcriptionally inactive cells owing to the tight compaction of their chromatin with protamine. However, sperm cells have been demonstrated to retain RNA polymerase subunits, chromatin remodellers, transcription factors, and parts of their chromatin remain in a less condensed, nucleosome-bound configuration. Consequently, some studies have suggested that sperm may be transcriptionally more active than previously assumed. Here, we tested this possibility by exposing mature human sperm to follicular fluid (FF), a bioactive liquid surrounding the oocyte. Using RNA sequencing, we first observed that FF exposure alters the sperm transcriptome. To resolve whether the observed upregulation of selected candidate genes resulted from the transcriptional activation of these genes in sperm, we labelled newly synthesized RNAs with 5-ethynyl uridine. Our results suggest that FF may trigger de novo transcription of sperm CXCL8 and CXCL3 genes and indicate that some follicular-fluid-derived transcripts are selectively transferred into sperm. Collectively, these findings suggest that specific sperm genes may become transcriptionally active in the presence of biologically relevant stimuli, potentially preparing sperm for fertilization and early embryo development. Furthermore, we envisage that activated sperm genes can have novel implications for the deeper mechanistic understanding of sexual selection.
